title: Quadtrees: adaptive spatial indexes

kcs.statement: A quadtree splits a region into four children whenever a node holds more than a set capacity (for example 100 places). Dense cities get deep, small cells and empty areas stay as large cells.

A quadtree is usually an in-memory structure rebuilt or updated on the server, while geohash strings fit into any database index. Quadtrees suit uneven density and geohash suits simple prefix queries.

problem_ideas: Insert 500 points into a quadtree with capacity 100 and predict the leaf count for a uniform spread.
Manhattan has 10,000 restaurants and a rural county has 10. Compare the cell sizes that result.
Estimate the memory for a quadtree indexing 200M places at 24 bytes each plus node overhead.
Drivers move every 4 seconds. Argue whether to update a quadtree in place or use geohash buckets.
Find the k nearest places by expanding to neighbouring quadtree nodes.
Choose between quadtree and geohash for Yelp (static places) and for Uber (moving drivers).
